bib.title: Program Induction by Rationale Generation: Learning to Solve and Explain Algebraic Word Problems

read.skipped: References skimmed only; no appendix exists

question: Can a model learn to solve algebraic word problems by generating a natural-language answer rationale together with the arithmetic program that produces it, when only question, rationale and answer are given?
hypothesis: Indirect supervision of program learning via answer rationales makes program induction feasible, where inducing programs directly from question-answer pairs is not.
contributions: A new dataset of more than 100,000 algebraic word problems with answers and natural-language rationales
A sequence-to-sequence model that generates instructions which, when executed, produce the rationale, and only then chooses the answer
A technique (heuristic search guided by the rationale) for inferring programs that generate a rationale and the answer

method.summary: A 2-layer LSTM decoder emits a latent program of typed instructions (operation, destination, arguments) that is executed to write the rationale tokens and the final option letter. Programs are unobserved, so the model maximises the probability of sampled programs that reproduce the rationale, with rationale-guided heuristic filtering and staged back-propagation.
method.task: multiple-choice algebra word problem solving with rationale generation

datasets.name: Algebra word problem dataset (not named in the paper)
datasets.size: 104,519 problems collected (34,202 seed + 70,318 crowdsourced); 100,949 train, 250 dev, 250 test
datasets.source: Seed problems from GMAT/GRE-style exam sites with rationales; further questions written by Mechanical Turk workers who rewrote one of 5 seed questions; licence not stated
datasets.preprocessing: Replicas of the 500 heldout problems removed from training manually using character-level Levenshtein nearest neighbours; avg tokens question+options+rationale: question 77.4, rationale 105.7; vocab 38,858 / 39,779

models.name: Program-generating seq2seq (Our Model)
models.architecture: 2-layer LSTM encoder-decoder, pointer-network copy from input and from output/memory via latent predictor network, 22 executable operations
models.vocab: 20,000 most frequent word types, rest unknown

other.operations: 22, of which 13 frequent math ops (Id, Add, Subtract, Multiply, Divide, Power, Log, Sqrt, Sine, Cosine, Tangent, Factorial, Choose)

models.name: Seq2Seq (Bahdanau et al. 2014), +Copy Input (Ling et al. 2016), +Copy Output (Merity et al. 2016)

training.objective: maximise sum of p(z|x) over sampled programs z in Z^(y) that execute to the reference rationale y (approximate marginal likelihood)

other.staged back-propagation: slices of K tokens of z (example K=100 for |z|=300); K value used in experiments not stated
other.program search: heuristic filter keeps instructions with at most one level of indirection (one intermediate value in memory)

inference.decoding: beam search, beam 200; stack-based decoder; hypotheses that fail on execution (e.g. log(0)) removed; after <EOR> only option letters A-E allowed
inference.samples: single run; number of seeds not stated

other.perplexity: model force-decoded to the reference rationale, taking the most likely program

metrics.name: Perplexity
metrics.definition: average sentence-level perplexity of the rationale; unknown token predicted when a model cannot generate a token

metrics.name: BLEU
metrics.definition: BLEU-4 between generated and reference rationale

metrics.name: Accuracy
metrics.definition: percentage of questions where chosen option matches correct option

eval.protocol: single evaluation on the 250-example test set; no seeds or significance test stated; chance is 20%

availability.data: inferred: dataset is the paper's contribution, but no release URL is given in the text

evidence.quote: We used a two-layer LSTM with a hidden size of H = 200, and word embeddings with size 200.

results.claim: The program-generating model reaches 36.4% accuracy while the three seq2seq baselines stay near the 20% chance level.
results.setup: 250-question test set, 5-option multiple-choice algebra word problems, 100,949 training problems; baselines also generate rationales
results.table: Table 3, row Our Model, column Accuracy

results.setup: 250-question test set, 5-option multiple-choice algebra word problems, 100,949 training problems, plain attention Seq2Seq
results.quote: all baseline models obtain values close to chance (20%), indicating that they are completely unable to solve the problem

results.claim: The model has the lowest rationale perplexity.
results.setup: 250-question test set, 5-option multiple-choice algebra word problems, 100,949 training problems
results.table: Table 3, row Our Model, column Perplexity

results.claim: The model has the highest rationale BLEU-4.
results.setup: 250-question test set, 5-option multiple-choice algebra word problems, 100,949 training problems
results.table: Table 3, row Our Model, column BLEU

results.claim: Correct answers are mostly simple problems solvable in one or two operations; complex rationales remain unsolved.
results.setup: 250-question test set, 5-option multiple-choice algebra word problems, 100,949 training problems
results.quote: In general, the problems we solve correctly correspond to simple problems that can be solved in one or two operations.

results.claim: The learner fails without rationales because the program search space is too unconstrained (asserted, no ablation reported).
results.quote: the learner we propose (which relies on a heuristic search;§4) fails to solve this task without modeling the rationales—the search space is too unconstrained.

results.claim: The rationale is a latent variable giving rise to the answer, argued to be more faithful than post-hoc explanations.
results.quote: the rationale is generated as a latent variable that gives rise to the answer—it is thus a more faithful representation of the steps used in computing the answer.

results.claim: Dataset size: 104,519 problems collected, 100,949 remain in training after filtering.
results.quote: In total, we collected 104,519 problems (34,202 seed problems and 70,318 crowdsourced problems).

limits: Authors concede that generating complex multi-step rationales correctly is still unsolved.
No ablation of rationale vs no rationale accuracy; the claim is prose only.
Single run on a 250-question test set; no seeds, confidence intervals or significance test.
Optimizer, learning rate, batch size, epochs, K for staged backprop and hardware are not stated.
Dataset is not named in the text and no release link is given.
Small LSTMs trained from scratch with supervised rationales; not prompting of pretrained LMs.

terms.definition: training on slices of K tokens of the program z to save memory, while the hidden state sequence h is still built for the whole sequence
crowdsourced problems where the natural language of question and rationale is only minimally altered from the seed
